metadata.naming_convention: Humanly meaningful hyphenated terms per DK preference. 2-letter abbreviations retained in 'abbreviation' field for backward compatibility.

tier_definitions.T1: Framework theories — neurally grounded, cross-domain, convergent multi-method support (10 frameworks)
tier_definitions.T1.5: Canonical domain theories with established authorship and formal reduction to T1 (4 theories: attention-restoration-theory, stress-recovery-theory, biophilia-hypothesis, prospect-refuge-theory)
tier_definitions.domain_theory: Additional domain theories assessed for entrenchment but not part of canonical T1.5 set

theories.formulation_reference: Foundational: Kandel (2001) Molecular basis of long-term potentiation; Damasio (1999) on neuromodulatory cascades; Dale et al. (1996) on neurotransmitter physiology. Key modern consolidations: Gruart et al. (2015) on dopamine/learning; Ciruela et al. (2016) on neuromodulatory networks.

justification.ECB: Dopamine, serotonin, acetylcholine, and cortisol pathways extensively confirmed across species through molecular biology, electrophysiology, behavioral pharmacology, and human neuroimaging. Hundreds of labs, thousands of studies with converging evidence on mechanism and function.
justification.PN: Predicted specific pharmacological effects (dopamine blockade → movement disorder, serotonin agonism → mood lift) confirmed before receptor cloning. Predicted dose-dependent effects on cognitive domains (working memory, exploration/exploitation). Predicted neuroendocrine-behavior links (cortisol → threat sensitivity).
justification.TP: Dose-response relationships rigorously characterized (e.g., inverted-U dopamine-performance curve). Quantitative receptor binding curves, receptor density maps. Timebase specified (dopamine reuptake ~100ms, serotonin ~5-10x slower). Boundary conditions well-defined (receptor subtype matters; brain region matters).
justification.CUC: Foundational to psychiatry, neuropharmacology, endocrinology. Textbook science. Psychiatric drugs (SSRIs, antipsychotics, stimulants) directly derived from theory. Integrated across neuroscience, endocrinology, evolutionary biology.
justification.CAS: Deeply connected to molecular biology (receptor genes, transporters), electrophysiology (channel states), neurochemistry (synthesis/metabolism), endocrinology (HPA axis), evolutionary biology (conservation across taxa).

theories.formulation_reference: Czeisler et al. (1999); Berson et al. (2002); circadian neuroscience as consolidated in Golombek & Rosenstein (2010)

justification.ECB: Hundreds of studies across species, methods (molecular, behavioral, physiological, neural), and independent labs. Core predictions about entrainment, phase-response curves, melatonin suppression all confirmed.
justification.PN: Predicted ipRGC role before Berson et al. (2002) discovery. Predicted blind-entrainment (Czeisler et al. 1995). Predicted spectral sensitivity peak ~480nm confirmed by action spectra.
justification.TP: Quantitative dose-response curves (lux × duration → melatonin suppression %), action spectra, phase-response curves, chronotype-specific predictions. Explicit boundary conditions (wavelength range, timescale).
justification.CUC: Textbook science. Nobel Prize 2017 (Hall, Rosbash, Young). Cross-disciplinary uptake (medicine, psychology, architecture, workplace design).
justification.CAS: Directly integrated with molecular biology (clock genes), neuroscience (SCN electrophysiology), endocrinology (melatonin, cortisol), evolutionary biology (circadian rhythms universal in multicellular organisms).

theories.formulation_reference: Tulving (1985) Episodic and semantic memory; Squire & Knowlton (1995); modern consolidation in Eichenbaum (2014)

justification.ECB: Episodic/semantic/procedural/working memory distinction extensively confirmed through dissociations in amnesia, neuroimaging, developmental psychology, and animal work. O'Keefe & Nadel place cells, Squire's patient H.M., extensive lesion and pharmacological work.
justification.PN: Predicted specific amnesia patterns (preserved procedural learning despite episodic amnesia; preserved semantic islands despite general forgetting) confirmed before mechanistic explanation. Predicted hippocampal-dependent binding of disparate information — confirmed by single-unit recording.
justification.TP: Quantitative characterization of memory functions: consolidation timescales (hours to years), decay curves (power law forgetting), hippocampal binding capacity. Explicit boundaries: hippocampus for new episodic, cortex for consolidated semantic; striatum for procedural.
justification.CUC: Textbook neuroscience. Widely adopted in cognitive psychology, neuroscience, education. Extensively debated (Tulving vs. others on episodic/semantic distinction; recent challenges from predictive processing view). Nobel-caliber foundational work.
justification.CAS: Deeply integrated with hippocampal neuroscience (place cells, grid cells, population coding), molecular neuroscience (synaptic plasticity, long-term potentiation), computational modeling (reinforcement learning architectures).

theories.formulation_reference: Tolman (1948) Cognitive maps in rats and men; O'Keefe & Nadel (1978); modern synthesis in Moser et al. (2015)

justification.ECB: Place cells, grid cells, head direction cells extensively confirmed across species (rodents, primates, humans via fMRI) and independent labs. Lynch's spatial imageability framework confirmed in human wayfinding. Convergent evidence from behavioral, electrophysiological, and imaging studies.
justification.PN: Tolman predicted cognitive maps before neural substrate was known — spectacularly confirmed by O'Keefe & Nadel place cell discovery. Predicted grid cells before Hafting et al. (2005) discovery — confirmed. Predicted environmental geometry computation — entorhinal boundary cells confirmed. Novel prediction of hippocampal sequence replay during sleep.
justification.TP: Quantitative characterization: place field sizes (20-100cm in rats), grid cell spacing ratios (1.4x), head direction tuning width. Allocentric coordinates specified. Computational models (Hopfield networks, continuous attractor models) with explicit parameters. Boundary conditions specified.
justification.CUC: Foundational in spatial cognition, neuroscience, AI (SLAM/robotics). Nobel Prize 2014 (O'Keefe, Moser, Moser). Extensively integrated across cognitive science, neuroscience, engineering, robotics.
justification.CAS: Deeply connected to hippocampal/entorhinal physiology, graph theory of cognitive spaces, computational neuroscience (path integration algorithms), robotics (simultaneous localization and mapping).

theories.formulation_reference: Meredith & Stein (1983); Stein & Stanford (2008); modern synthesis in Klemen & Chambers (2012)

justification.ECB: McGurk effect (auditory-visual speech) confirmed across cultures. Spatial/temporal rules for multisensory enhancement extensively tested in superior colliculus and cortical studies. Cross-modal attention effects well-replicated. Superadditivity in SC multisensory neurons confirmed.
justification.PN: Predicted that visual dominance would depend on stimulus properties, not absolute modality ranking (Colavita effect reframed as unisensory capture). Predicted inverse effectiveness — predicted that weak unisensory stimuli would show greater multisensory enhancement — extensively confirmed. Predicted temporal window of integration.
justification.TP: Quantified spatial (±20-45° visual-auditory), temporal (±100-300ms), and contextual interaction rules. Calculated enhancement ratios (superadditivity measured as response > sum of unisensory). Boundary conditions explicit: applies strongest in SC and some cortical areas.
justification.CUC: Textbook neuroscience. Widely taught. Actively extended (crossmodal plasticity, audiovisual illusions, courtship signals in frogs). Strong empirical engagement. Well-established paradigms (SC recordings, psychophysics).
justification.CAS: Deeply connected to midbrain physiology (SC structure), cortical microcircuits, temporal coordination mechanisms (oscillations). Computational models (biologically plausible neural networks) well-developed.

theories.formulation_reference: Friston (2010) The free-energy principle; Clark (2013) Whatever next?; Bubic et al. (2010) Prediction, cognition and the brain

justification.ECB: Prediction error signals confirmed in visual cortex (MMN), auditory cortex, motor system, and dopamine neurons. Mismatch negativity paradigm shows robust replicable effects. Free energy principle provides unifying framework. Extensive evidence from electrophysiology, imaging, and pharmacology.
justification.PN: Predicted mismatch negativity as index of prediction error — confirmed before free energy formalism. Predicted surprise-dependent learning and model updating. Predicted that brain computes prediction errors about sensory consequences of actions — confirmed in motor learning and sensorimotor adaptation experiments.
justification.TP: Quantitative predictions possible via free energy functional (Variational Free Energy, KL divergence between generative and recognition models). Bayesian inference mathematics well-specified. But meta-theory very general — applicable to any learning, hence difficult to falsify in strict sense.
justification.CUC: Major paradigm in cognitive neuroscience and philosophy of mind. Enormous literature (thousands of papers). Extensively debated (Clark vs. Colombo on scope; Bruineberg et al. on ecological embeddedness). Actively extended (psychiatric applications, robotics).
justification.CAS: Deep connections to Bayesian statistics, information theory, control theory, machine learning (backpropagation), and computational neuroscience. Some tensions with ecological psychology (too internalist view of prediction).

theories.formulation_reference: Raichle et al. (2001); Fox & Raichle (2007); modern synthesis in Buckner et al. (2008)

justification.ECB: DMN/TPN (Task-Positive Network) anticorrelation confirmed in resting-state fMRI across labs. Medial prefrontal-posterior cingulate connectivity well-documented. Creative cognition link (Beaty et al.) supported. Mind-wandering neuroimaging confirmed.
justification.PN: Predicted mind-wandering involves default mode activity — confirmed by experience sampling + fMRI. Predicted that DMN deactivation during task performance is related to task difficulty/attention demand — confirmed. Predicted default mode involves social/mentalizing: implicated in theory-of-mind — confirmed.
justification.TP: Network dynamics quantifiable via connectivity strength (correlation matrices, graph metrics). Some quantitative predictions (e.g., DMN strength predicts mind-wandering propensity, behavioral correlations with task performance). But exact computational mechanism of creativity from DMN remains qualitative.
justification.CUC: Major paradigm in functional neuroimaging. Hundreds of papers. Widely taught in cognitive neuroscience. Actively debated (is DMN functionally unified or multiple subnetworks? causal role in creativity vs. epiphenomenal?).
justification.CAS: Deeply integrated with network neuroscience (graph theory, modularity), resting-state neuroimaging methodology, and creativity research. Some connections to attention networks and intrinsic brain organization.

theories.formulation_reference: Kahneman & Tversky (1974) Judgment under uncertainty; Kahneman (2011) Thinking, fast and slow; Evans & Stanovich (2013) modern synthesis

justification.ECB: System 1/2 distinction confirmed by dissociations in judgment, decision-making, and implicit/explicit learning. Implicit attitude measures (IAT) show System 1 effects. Dual-task interference patterns confirm capacity-limited System 2. Cognitive load manipulations replicate.
justification.PN: Predicted base-rate neglect, anchoring, availability bias — confirmed. Predicted implicit/explicit dissociations in attitude learning and memory — confirmed. Predicted that System 2 could override System 1 — confirmed by debiasing studies. Predicted individual differences (cognitive reflection) — confirmed.
justification.TP: Qualitative System 1/System 2 distinction; some quantitative predictions in judgment and decision-making (weighting functions in prospect theory). Neural dissociation increasingly documented but exact mapping debated (amygdala/prefrontal, but not clean). Boundary conditions somewhat vague.
justification.CUC: Kahneman Nobel Prize 2002. Textbook psychology. Extensively applied (behavioral economics, policy design, debiasing). Actively debated (dual-system vs. single-system models; neural implementation).
justification.CAS: Connected to executive control neuroscience (prefrontal cortex), limbic affect systems (amygdala), reward systems (ventromedial PFC). Some debate about whether distinct neural systems correspond to logical dual-process distinction.

theories.formulation_reference: Barrett (2006) Emotions as natural kinds; Barrett (2017) How emotions are made; modern neuroscience in Craig (2015) on interoception

justification.ECB: Interoceptive accuracy studies show body-emotion correlations (Barrett & Adolph, 2007). Body budget concept (Damasio-style homeostasis) empirically supported. Allostatic load as predictor of health outcomes confirmed. Emotions as constructed (not basic) supported by cross-cultural variation studies.
justification.PN: Predicted emotional-interoceptive overlap (anterior insula as hub) — confirmed by imaging. Predicted that interoceptive errors correlate with emotional disorders — supported. Predicted emotions are culturally variable constructions — confirmed by anthropological/linguistic studies (Barrett, Lindquist).
justification.TP: Allostatic load quantifiable via multi-system physiological measures. Body budget framework somewhat qualitative. Interoceptive accuracy measurable (heartbeat detection tasks, etc.). But exact mapping between interoceptive signals and emotional category remains probabilistic, not deterministic.
justification.CUC: Barrett's constructionist theory widely debated (James Russell, others argue basic emotions exist). Increasingly influential in affective neuroscience. Integrated into psychiatry/clinical psychology. Critique: challenges classical emotion categories.
justification.CAS: Connected to insula physiology, anterior cingulate function, vagal afferent signaling. Integrated with theories of self and embodiment. Some tension with evolutionary psychology (basic emotions view).

theories.formulation_reference: Gibbs (2005) Embodiment and cognitive science; Lakoff & Johnson (1980) Metaphors we live by; modern neuroscience in Glenberg (2010)

justification.ECB: Action-perception coupling confirmed: mirror neurons (Rizzolatti), motor simulation during language comprehension (Pulvermüller), affordance priming effects (Tucker & Ellis). But mirror neuron interpretation debated. Motor cortex activation during language confirmed but mechanism unclear.
justification.PN: Predicted that understanding action language would activate motor cortex — confirmed by TMS/fMRI. Predicted that preventing hand movement would impair manipulable-object understanding — partially confirmed. Predicted embodied metaphors in abstract thought — supported by linguistic evidence (Lakoff & Johnson).
justification.TP: Specific motor activation patterns measurable and quantifiable. But theory scope not always clear: does all cognition require embodiment or just some domains? Quantitative boundary conditions not well-specified. Computational models less developed than for symbolic approaches.
justification.CUC: Widely taught in cognitive science, linguistics, embodied AI. Actively debated (weak vs. strong embodiment; neuroplasticity challenges motor cortex specificity). Growing integration with robotics and AI.
justification.CAS: Connected to motor neuroscience, mirror neuron system, sensorimotor cortex. Some tensions with abstract cognition research and productivity of symbolic systems. Growing integration with robotics and grounded AI.

theories.formulation_reference: Kaplan, S. (1995). The restorative benefits of nature: Toward an integrative framework. Journal of Environmental Psychology, 15(3), 169-182.

justification.ECB: Basic restoration effect confirmed across many studies. Ohly et al. (2016) meta-analysis found modest but consistent effects. Specific component predictions (soft fascination, compatibility) less well tested independently.
justification.PN: Distinction between directed and involuntary attention generated some novel predictions about non-nature restoration (museums, meditation spaces). But most 'predictions' elaborate motivating observations.
justification.TP: Four qualitative components (being away, extent, soft fascination, compatibility) without quantitative thresholds. No dose-response specification. No explicit scope boundaries.
justification.CUC: Widely used in environmental psychology. Regularly critiqued (Joye & van den Berg 2011, Hartig et al. 2014). Survived with modifications.
justification.CAS: Compatible with attention network neuroscience but not directly derived from it. No specific neural mechanism proposed for 'soft fascination'.

theories.formulation_reference: Ulrich, R. S. (1983). Aesthetic and affective response to natural environment. In Altman & Wohlwill (Eds.), Behavior and the natural environment.

justification.ECB: Core finding — nature views reduce stress — well-replicated. Specific 'evolutionary hard-wired' claim less well tested.
justification.PN: Hospital window study (Ulrich 1984) was essentially the motivating observation, though it came after initial theory. Limited genuinely novel predictions.
justification.TP: Specifies that stress reduction is faster with nature than urban. Does not quantify dose-response or individual differences.
justification.CUC: Widely cited, regularly paired with ART. Some critique that it overlaps with ART without clear differentiation (Hartig et al. 2014).
justification.CAS: Compatible with ANS physiology. Evolutionary claim loosely supported but not rigorously grounded.

theories.formulation_reference: Kellert, S. R., & Wilson, E. O. (Eds.). (1993). The biophilia hypothesis. Island Press.

justification.ECB: Nature preference studies support broad claim. Core commitment — preference is innate vs. culturally learned — largely untested. Twin studies absent.
justification.PN: Theory constructed to explain existing observations. Predictions about phobias, landscape preference are elaborations of motivating data, not genuinely novel.
justification.TP: Qualitative: 'humans have innate tendency to affiliate with living systems.' No quantitative predictions, thresholds, or scope limits.
justification.CUC: Widely cited in environmental design and biophilic architecture. Critiqued by Joye & De Block (2011). Innate/learned distinction unresolved.
justification.CAS: Compatible with evolutionary psychology in principle but lacks specific genetic, neural, or developmental substrates.

theories.formulation_reference: Appleton, J. (1975). The experience of landscape. Wiley.

justification.ECB: Some landscape preference studies support prospect-refuge predictions (Stamps 2005; Dosen & Ostwald 2016). But effect sizes are modest and confounded with openness, complexity, naturalness.
justification.PN: Theory constructed to explain existing landscape preferences. Predictions (savanna preference, edge-space preference) overlap with motivating data. Few genuinely surprising predictions.
justification.TP: Qualitative: 'people prefer views with prospect (open vista) and refuge (enclosed shelter).' No quantitative thresholds for what counts as prospect vs. refuge. Scope undefined.
justification.CUC: Widely cited in architectural theory and landscape architecture. Less empirically engaged than ART/SRT. Critiques include difficulty of operationalization.
justification.CAS: Loosely compatible with evolutionary psychology (predator avoidance). Lacks neural or physiological substrate. No connection to established attention or stress systems.

theories.formulation_reference: Kaplan, S., & Kaplan, R. (1989). The experience of nature: A psychological perspective. Cambridge University Press.

justification.ECB: Coherence-complexity and legibility-mystery dimensions tested in multiple studies. Results generally supportive but effect sizes variable. Mystery dimension inconsistently supported (Stamps 2004).
justification.PN: Predicted that legibility and mystery would independently predict preference — partially confirmed. But 2×2 matrix was constructed from observed patterns, limiting novelty.
justification.TP: Four named dimensions (coherence, complexity, legibility, mystery) but without quantitative scales. No specification of how dimensions combine or trade off.
justification.CUC: Widely taught in environmental psychology. Frequently cited. Some critique that mystery and complexity are confounded. Less empirical engagement than ART.
justification.CAS: Some connection to Berlyne's arousal theory (complexity). No direct neural or physiological grounding.

theories.formulation_reference: de Dear, R. J., & Brager, G. S. (1998). Developing an adaptive model of thermal comfort and preference. ASHRAE Transactions, 104(1), 145-167.

justification.ECB: ASHRAE RP-884 database (21,000 observations, 160 buildings). Adaptive model confirmed across climates and cultures. Incorporated into ASHRAE Standard 55 and EN 15251.
justification.PN: Predicted that comfort temperature tracks outdoor running-mean temperature — genuinely novel vs. static PMV model (Fanger 1970). Predicted that naturally ventilated buildings have wider comfort zones — confirmed.
justification.TP: Quantitative: T_comfort = 0.31 × T_outdoor_running_mean + 17.8°C. Specifies acceptable ranges (±3.5°C for 80% acceptability). Explicit scope: applies to naturally ventilated buildings, not sealed HVAC.
justification.CUC: Incorporated into international standards (ASHRAE 55, EN 15251). Strong industry uptake. Debated by PMV proponents but has largely won the empirical argument for naturally ventilated contexts.
justification.CAS: Compatible with thermal physiology (acclimatization mechanisms well-understood). Compatible with behavioral adaptation literature. Good mechanistic grounding in thermoregulation.

theories.formulation_reference: Csikszentmihalyi, M. (1990). Flow: The psychology of optimal experience. Harper & Row.

justification.ECB: Extensively studied across domains (sports, music, work, gaming). Experience Sampling Method (ESM) studies broadly confirm challenge-skill balance prediction. Nakamura & Csikszentmihalyi (2009) review.
justification.PN: Predicted that flow would occur in any activity with clear goals, immediate feedback, and challenge-skill balance — confirmed in diverse domains beyond original artistic/athletic contexts. Predicted autotelic personality differences.
justification.TP: Specifies conditions (challenge-skill balance, clear goals, immediate feedback) but does not quantify thresholds. The 'channel model' (flow between anxiety and boredom) is qualitative. Some quantification via Flow Short Scale.
justification.CUC: Major paradigm in positive psychology. Textbook inclusion. Extensively debated (Abuhamdeh 2020, critique of channel model). Very high citation count (~80,000 for the 1990 book).
justification.CAS: Compatible with intrinsic motivation research (Deci & Ryan). Some neural correlates proposed (transient hypofrontality, Dietrich 2004) but not well-established. Compatible with optimal arousal theory.

theories.formulation_reference: Reber, R., Schwarz, N., & Winkielman, P. (2004). Processing fluency and aesthetic pleasure: Is beauty in the perceiver's processing experience? Personality and Social Psychology Review, 8(4), 364-382.

justification.ECB: Fluency-preference link confirmed across many paradigms (mere exposure, symmetry, prototypicality, contrast). Alter & Oppenheimer (2009) review covers broad confirmation.
justification.PN: Predicted that disfluency manipulations (hard-to-read fonts) would reduce preference — confirmed. Predicted that fluency would affect truth judgments (Reber & Schwarz 1999) — confirmed. Genuinely novel: not obvious that ease of processing would affect aesthetic and epistemic judgments.
justification.TP: Quantitative predictions possible (fluency is measurable via RT, identification thresholds). But theory does not specify when fluency preference reverses (disfluency-as-signal-of-depth). Scope partially specified.
justification.CUC: Well-established in cognitive psychology. Regularly extended and critiqued. Debate about boundary conditions (when does disfluency become preferred?).
justification.CAS: Strong connections: perceptual processing speed (cognitive psychology), neural repetition suppression (neuroscience), prototype theory (categorization). Good mechanistic grounding.

theories.formulation_reference: Hall, E. T. (1966). The hidden dimension. Doubleday.

justification.ECB: Four distance zones (intimate, personal, social, public) confirmed across many cultures with variations. Sorokowska et al. (2017) — 42 countries, N>9,000. Cultural variation well-documented.
justification.PN: Distance zones were derived from observation — limited novelty. Some novel predictions: crowding stress depends on perceived invasion of personal space, not density per se (Stokols 1972). Cultural variation in zones was predicted.
justification.TP: Quantitative: specific distance ranges for each zone (intimate <0.45m, personal 0.45-1.2m, social 1.2-3.6m, public >3.6m). Cultural variation parameterized. More precise than most environmental theories.
justification.CUC: Foundational in environmental psychology and architecture. Widely taught, extensively cited (~6,200 citations). Critiques focus on cultural oversimplification.
justification.CAS: Compatible with ethology (territorial behavior). Some neural correlates (peripersonal space neurons). Compatible with stress physiology (invasion → cortisol).

theories.formulation_reference: Tolman, E. C. (1948). Cognitive maps in rats and men. Psychological Review, 55(4), 189-208; Lynch, K. (1960). The image of the city. MIT Press.

justification.ECB: Extensive confirmation from both animal (O'Keefe & Nadel 1978, place cells) and human (fMRI, virtual navigation) studies. Lynch's 5 elements (paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks) well-supported in urban cognition.
justification.PN: Tolman predicted that rats form spatial representations beyond stimulus-response chains — confirmed spectacularly by place cells and grid cells. Lynch predicted that imageability predicts wayfinding — confirmed. Nobel Prize 2014 (O'Keefe, Moser & Moser) for place/grid cells.
justification.TP: Animal work is quantitative (place field sizes, grid cell spacing). Human/architectural application is more qualitative (Lynch's 5 elements lack quantitative thresholds). Moderate overall.
justification.CUC: Foundational in spatial cognition, neuroscience, and urban planning. Nobel Prize 2014. Extensively debated (allocentric vs. egocentric, cognitive map vs. cognitive graph).
justification.CAS: Deeply integrated with hippocampal neuroscience, computational modeling (SLAM algorithms), evolutionary biology (spatial navigation as conserved function).

theories.formulation_reference: Altman, I., & Low, S. M. (Eds.). (1992). Place attachment. Plenum Press; Scannell, L., & Gifford, R. (2010). Defining place attachment. Journal of Environmental Psychology, 30(1), 1-10.

justification.ECB: Place attachment scales (Williams & Vaske 2003) show reliable measurement. Correlations with well-being, pro-environmental behavior confirmed. But causal direction unclear (does attachment cause well-being or vice versa?).
justification.PN: Theory mostly describes and categorizes existing observations about people-place bonds. Few genuinely novel predictions. Scannell & Gifford (2010) tripartite model (person, process, place) is organizational, not predictive.
justification.TP: Tripartite model names components but does not specify quantitative relationships. No threshold for 'attachment.' No dose-response for how place features produce attachment.
justification.CUC: Widely cited in environmental psychology and planning. Active research community. Some critique of conceptual overlap with sense of place, place identity.
justification.CAS: Some connection to attachment theory (Bowlby) but the analogy is contested. Compatible with identity theory (Proshansky 1978). Weak neural grounding.

theories.formulation_reference: Altman, I. (1975). The environment and social behavior: Privacy, personal space, territory, crowding. Brooks/Cole.

justification.ECB: Privacy as optimization (desired vs. achieved) supported in workplace and residential studies. Sundstrom et al. (1980) office studies confirm. Open-plan office critique literature broadly supports.
justification.PN: Predicted that both too-much and too-little privacy would produce stress — the optimization/dialectic model was somewhat novel vs. simple 'more privacy = better.' Predicted that privacy mechanisms are culturally variable.
justification.TP: Specifies a dialectical process (desired vs. achieved privacy) and multiple mechanisms (personal space, territory, verbal/nonverbal behavior). But no quantitative thresholds. Cultural variation acknowledged but not parameterized.
justification.CUC: Foundational in environment-behavior studies. Widely taught. Less actively debated than ART/SRT — somewhat taken for granted.
justification.CAS: Compatible with stress and coping literature (Lazarus & Folkman). Some connection to self-regulation. Limited neural grounding.

theories.formulation_reference: Friston, K. (2010) for general PP; Clark, A. (2013) for cognitive extension; Vuust & Witek (2014) for music-specific application.

justification.ECB: Core prediction-error claims confirmed in visual/auditory cortex. Mismatch negativity paradigm supports. But broad 'brain as prediction machine' is hard to falsify.
justification.PN: Predicted specific neural signatures (MMN in novel contexts). Predicted action-perception computational unity. Music-specific: predicted groove from syncopation-driven prediction error (Witek et al. 2014).
justification.TP: Quantitative in specific domains (free energy, Bayesian inference). Music application specifies information-theoretic surprise. But meta-theory extremely general.
justification.CUC: Major paradigm in neuroscience and philosophy of mind. Actively debated (Bruineberg et al. 2018, Colombo & Series 2012). Enormous literature.
justification.CAS: Deeply connected to Bayesian statistics, information theory, control theory. Some tension with ecological psychology.
